Part A — Examples of Conditional Statements.

Example A: if ... else. Choose between two outcomes for a single value.

```{r}

score <- 78

if (score >= 75) {
  print("Passed")
} else {
  print("Failed")
}

```

Example B: if ... else if ... else. Use it when there are more than two outcomes. R checks from top to bottom and stops at the first condition that is TRUE.


```{r}

score <- 86

if (score >= 90) {
  print("Excellent")
} else if (score >= 80) {
  print("Good")
} else if (score >= 75) {
  print("Fair")
} else {
  print("Needs Improvement")
}

```


Example C: ifelse() for a whole vector. if works on one value at a time. ifelse() checks every element of a vector at once, which is what you need for a column of data.

```{r}

scores <- c(92, 68, 75, 81, 59)
ifelse(scores >= 75, "Passed", "Failed")

```

Example D: combining conditions. Use & when both conditions must be true and | when at least one must be true.

```{r}

grade <- 91
attendance <- 95

if (grade >= 90 & attendance >= 90) {
  print("Honors candidate")
}

```

Question #5

What is the difference between if and ifelse()? When would you choose each one?

  For me, the biggest difference comes down to single decisions vs. whole vectors. I think of if / else as a traffic director for a single condition—when I'm checking one value or deciding which block of code to run next, if feels cleaner and more intentional. Plus, if you accidentally hand if a vector with multiple elements, R pushes back instead of quietly guessing across every item.

  On the other hand, I reach for ifelse() whenever I'm working on a whole vector or column and want a quick, element-by-element label or value back—like tagging scores as "Pass" or "Fail" without writing a loop.

  How I choose in practice: If I'm controlling program flow or checking one condition at a time, I go with if / else. If I'm transforming a vector of values all at once (and their types match cleanly), ifelse() is my go-to—and if things get messy with multiple conditions or strict types, I'll often consider dplyr::case_when() in bigger scripts.


Part C: Importing the CSV File.

Scenario. You are the data assistant of Mabini National High School. The registrar gave you students_grades.csv, which holds quiz, midterm, and final exam scores and attendance for 15 students. Your job is to compute each student’s final grade, decide who passed, assign grade remarks, flag students at risk, identify honors candidates, and send the cleaned results back to the registrar as CSV files.

The csv file can be downloaded here: Students Grades [https://drive.google.com/file/d/1PkVDjLngc95cFl9Z8lhzYiOy1UDXEPGL/view?usp=sharing]

The registrar’s file has one row per student and these columns:

Column	Meaning	Type
StudentID	Unique student number	Number
Name	Student’s full name	Text
Section	Class section (A, B, or C)	Text
Quiz	Average quiz score, 0 to 100	Number
Midterm	Midterm exam score, 0 to 100	Number
Final	Final exam score, 0 to 100	Number
Attendance	Attendance rate in percent	Number

f. Applying Conditional Statements
The registrar uses these rules. Each task adds a new column to grades.

Rule	Condition
Final grade	30% Quiz + 30% Midterm + 40% Final
Result	Passed if the final grade is 75 or higher, otherwise Failed
Remarks	90 and above Excellent; 85 to 89 Very Good; 80 to 84 Good; 75 to 79 Fair; below 75 Needs Improvement
Attendance flag	At Risk if attendance is below 80, otherwise OK
Honors	Yes if the final grade is 90 or higher and attendance is 90 or higher
Missing scores	Any student with a missing score is marked Incomplete


f.1 Compute the final grade.** Any arithmetic with NA gives NA, so the student with the missing midterm will have NA as a final grade. This is expected.

```{r}

grades$FinalGrade <- 0.30 * grades$Quiz + 0.30 * grades$Midterm + 0.40 * grades$Final

```




f.2 Pass or fail.** Check for NA first, because NA >= 75 gives NA, not TRUE or FALSE.

```{r}

grades$Result <- ifelse(
  is.na(grades$FinalGrade),
  "Incomplete",
  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 75, "Passed", "Failed")
)

```


f.3 Grade remarks.** Replace each ___ with the correct cutoff or label, then change eval=FALSE to eval=TRUE in the chunk header.

```{r}
eval=TRUE

grades$Remarks <- ifelse(
  is.na(grades$FinalGrade),
  "Incomplete",
  ifelse(
    grades$FinalGrade >= 90, "Excellent",
    ifelse(
      grades$FinalGrade >= 85, "Very Good",
      ifelse(
        grades$FinalGrade >= 80, "Good",
        ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 75, "Fair", "Needs Improvement")
      )
    )
  )
)

```


f.4 Attendance flag.** Write one ifelse() statement that creates a column AttendanceFlag with "At Risk" when Attendance is below 80 and "OK" otherwise.

```{r}

grades$AttendanceFlag <- ifelse(grades$Attendance < 80, "At Risk", "OK")

```

f.5 Honors candidates.** Write one ifelse() statement that creates a column Honors with "Yes" or "No". Use & to require both a final grade of 90 or higher and attendance of 90 or higher. Students with a missing final grade must get "No". Hint: use !is.na(grades$FinalGrade) as the first condition.

```{r}

grades$Honors <- ifelse(
  !is.na(grades$FinalGrade) & grades$FinalGrade >= 90 & grades$Attendance >= 90,
  "Yes",
  "No"
)

```


f.6 if ... else if inside a loop.** ifelse() works on a whole column, but a plain if handles one value at a time. To use if on a column you must loop over the rows.

```{r}

remarks_loop <- character(nrow(grades))

for (i in seq_len(nrow(grades))) {
  fg <- grades$FinalGrade[i]
  if (is.na(fg)) {
    remarks_loop[i] <- "Incomplete"
  } else if (fg >= 90) {
    remarks_loop[i] <- "Excellent"
  } else if (fg >= 85) {
    remarks_loop[i] <- "Very Good"
  } else if (fg >= 80) {
    remarks_loop[i] <- "Good"
  } else if (fg >= 75) {
    remarks_loop[i] <- "Fair"
  } else {
    remarks_loop[i] <- "Needs Improvement"
  }
}

grades$Remarks <- remarks_loop

```


f.7 Now try if (grades$FinalGrade >= 75) print("Passed") on its own in the Console. Explain the error or warning R gives and why the loop version avoids it.

  When I typed (grades$FinalGrade >= 75) print("Passed") into the Console in Posit Cloud, R gave me Error: unexpected symbol in "(grades$FinalGrade >= 75) print" because I wrapped the condition in parentheses instead of writing a proper if () statement and missed a line break or semicolon between two separate expressions ((grades$FinalGrade >= 75) and print("Passed")). Even if I fix that syntax and write if (grades$FinalGrade >= 75) print("Passed"), a plain if still only expects a single TRUE or FALSE value of length 1 rather than a 15-element vector with an NA (so R would complain about condition length greater than 1 or an NA condition). My for loop avoids those issues because I put each statement on its own line inside { ... }, pull one student's score at a time (fg <- grades$FinalGrade[i]) as a single value, and check if (is.na(fg)) first before doing any comparison.


f.8 Summarize your results.** Then write in comments how many students passed, how many are At Risk, and how many are honors candidates. Compare with a seatmate.

```{r}

table(grades$Result, useNA = "ifany")
table(grades$AttendanceFlag, useNA = "ifany")
table(grades$Honors, useNA = "ifany")

```

f.9 Check grades should now have 12 columns (7 original plus FinalGrade, Result, Remarks, AttendanceFlag, Honors).

```{r}

ncol(grades)
names(grades)
ncol(grades) == 12

```


Part D: Exporting Results to .csv.

The registrar needs three files: the full processed table, a list of at-risk students, and a list of honors candidates.

Question #7

A. Export the full processed table.** The argument row.names = FALSE stops R from adding an extra numbering column.

```{r}

# Ensure AttendanceFlag and Honors exist if not yet added
if (!"AttendanceFlag" %in% names(grades)) {
  grades$AttendanceFlag <- ifelse(grades$Attendance < 80, "At Risk", "OK")
}
if (!"Honors" %in% names(grades)) {
  grades$Honors <- ifelse(
    !is.na(grades$FinalGrade) & grades$FinalGrade >= 90 & grades$Attendance >= 90,
    "Yes",
    "No"
  )
}

write.csv(grades, "students_grades_processed.csv", row.names = FALSE)

```


B. Export the at-risk students.** The file is written only when there is at least one at-risk student.

```{r}

at_risk <- grades[!is.na(grades$AttendanceFlag) & grades$AttendanceFlag == "At Risk", ]

if (nrow(at_risk) > 0) {
  write.csv(at_risk, "at_risk_students.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  message("Wrote at_risk_students.csv with ", nrow(at_risk), " student(s).")
} else {
  message("No at-risk students found; at_risk_students.csv was not written.")
}

```


C. Export the honors list.

Create a data frame honors with only the rows where Honors is "Yes".
Keep only these columns: StudentID, Name, Section, FinalGrade, Attendance. Hint: grades[rows_condition, c("StudentID", "Name")].

Use an if ... else statement to export it as honors_list.csv, or print a message if the list is empty.

```{r}

honors <- grades[
  !is.na(grades$Honors) & grades$Honors == "Yes",
  c("StudentID", "Name", "Section", "FinalGrade", "Attendance")
]

if (nrow(honors) > 0) {
  write.csv(honors, "honors_list.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  message("Wrote honors_list.csv with ", nrow(honors), " candidate(s).")
} else {
  message("Honors list is empty; honors_list.csv was not written.")
}

```

proc_check <- read.csv("students_grades_processed.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
dim(proc_check)

Question #8

How does the missing midterm appear in the exported file?

What would the file look like without row.names = FALSE? Try it with a temporary file name and compare.

```{r}

temp_with_rownames <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write.csv(grades, temp_with_rownames, row.names = TRUE)

with_rn_df <- read.csv(temp_with_rownames, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
head(with_rn_df, 5)
unlink(temp_with_rownames)

```

1. Missing midterm in CSV: Bea Navarro's missing Midterm (NA in R) is exported as an empty field (blank cell between commas, e.g., ,,) in the CSV, and R reads a blank field back as NA when imported with read.csv().

2. Without row.names = FALSE: R includes an extra unnamed/X column of row numbers ("1", "2", ..., "15") at the front of the CSV, which shifts column positions and can create an extra "X" column when read back in.


Checkpoint. Your folder should now contain students_grades.csv plus students_grades_processed.csv, at_risk_students.csv, and honors_list.csv.

B. Use nested ifelse() statements. Test the missing grade first, then Full, then Partial

```{r}

grades$Scholarship <- ifelse(
  is.na(grades$FinalGrade),
  "Pending",
  ifelse(
    grades$FinalGrade >= 95 & grades$Attendance >= 90,
    "Full",
    ifelse(
      grades$FinalGrade >= 85 & grades$Attendance >= 90,
      "Partial",
      "None"
    )
  )
)

```

Question #10

Answer in one or two sentences each, as comments.

1. Why did you check is.na() before comparing the final grade to a number?

```{r}

  #I checked is.na() first because comparing an NA value against a number gives NA instead of a clear TRUE or FALSE, which can mess up my conditions or cause errors. Catching missing grades early lets me handle incomplete records cleanly before any score comparisons run.

```


In Task 3.2, what would happen if the Failed condition were placed before the Incomplete condition?

```{r}

#In my view, putting Failed ahead of Incomplete makes the logic harder to follow and creates a risk of misclassifying missing grades if the condition order isn't written carefully. Checking for NA first keeps incomplete records separate before I test who passed or failed.

```

When is ifelse() the better choice than if ... else, and when is if ... else better?

```{r}

#I reach for ifelse() when I want to assign values across a whole column or vector all at once, one element at a time. On the other hand, I use if ... else when I'm controlling the flow of my script based on a single true-or-false check, like seeing if a file exists or if a table has rows before writing a CSV.

```


Why is it useful to read an exported CSV back into R?

```{r}

#Reading the file back in lets me make sure my export actually worked and didn't drop rows, add extra index columns, or change how missing values look. To me, it's the easiest way to double-check that what I saved matches what I intended to send out.

```
